newsitem.title: USA: Babbitt impressed by oil work in Alaska.
newsitem.headline: Babbitt impressed by oil work in Alaska.

text.p: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt Monday said he was impressed with oil firms' environmental progress in the Arctic, a factor he would weigh in deciding whether to open Alaska's "last frontier" to drilling.

Babbitt returned last week from a four-day tour of the area in and around the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska, which is just west of some of the biggest oil fields in North America that make up about a quarter of U.S. oil production.

"My task is to weigh whether or not there is some way of accommodating both the traditional way of life, the subsistence economy, and oil development," he said in an interview on National Public Radio's "Diane Rehm Show".

"Our premise with most resource development is that if you do it right it ought to be possible," he said. "What the oil companies show me up there is the way in which they have cleaned up their act over the last 30 years, and some of it's very impressive."

In an interview in which he attacked oil and coal companies for using their lobbying power in a "conspiracy" to battle an international climate change treaty that might force cuts in fossil fuel use, Babbitt had some praise for oil companies' efforts to preserve fragile land in Alaska.
Companies had found ways to avoid building roads, which he said was an important step toward saving the Arctic landscape and not driving away animals that the native villages in the area needed.

"They're now drilling oil wells without building roads," he said, explaining that the companies use ice roads when the tundra is frozen and get out when the ice melts and the land comes to life. "They even use ice for drilling pads."
Babbitt said villagers complained they had been cut off from hunting in existing oil fields, but he added that caribou herds apparently had not been harmed by oil development.
"The existing development suggests that the caribou herds may have some kind of coexistence capability," he said.
But he said a lot of migratory birds that breed in Alaska in the summer appeared to be very sensitive to the oil work.
"Maybe you can say you should have limited prospecting and drilling n some places but not others," he said.
